title: Exploring Electricity Supply-Mix Scenarios to 2030
summary: Develops three capacity scenarios for India's power system to 2030 — a Current Policy Scenario, a Current Trajectory Scenario, and a High RE Scenario — and compares them on capacity mix, generation, LCOE, system cost, and flexibility needs. Renewables emerge as the cheapest incremental generation source in all three, but the High RE Scenario carries the largest daily and seasonal balancing challenge.
recommendations: Prioritize development of system flexibility (storage, demand response, flexible thermal operation) alongside renewable capacity targets, rather than treating capacity addition and flexibility as separate problems. Track and manage the emerging surplus/deficit swings — daytime solar surplus and evening peak deficits — before they constrain further RE growth.
conclusion: A high-renewables pathway to 2030 is technically feasible and can be achieved at close to the same system cost as coal-heavy alternatives, once the additional cost of flexibility is included. The main risk is not capital cost but the growing operational challenge of balancing supply and demand at high VRE penetration.

title: Developing a Roadmap to a Flexible, Low-carbon Indian Electricity System: Interim Findings
summary: Interim findings exploring how India can integrate very high shares of wind and solar through an integrated approach combining demand management, dispatchable-fleet adaptation, and energy storage. Finds India can integrate 390 GW of wind and solar by 2030 — over 40% above the then-current trajectory — at lower cost than business as usual.
recommendations: Pursue an integrated flexibility strategy rather than isolated fixes: combine demand-side management, adaptation of the existing dispatchable (coal/hydro) fleet, and storage deployment together, since none alone is sufficient at high RE penetration.
conclusion: Higher renewable integration than currently targeted is achievable at lower cost, provided flexibility investment keeps pace with capacity addition — flexibility, not generation capacity, is the binding constraint.

title: Policy Paper on Solar PV Manufacturing in India: Silicon Ingot & Wafer – PV Cell – PV Module
summary: A policy paper examining India's solar PV manufacturing value chain — from silicon ingot and wafer production through cell and module manufacturing — assessing the domestic industry's competitiveness and the policy support needed to build capacity across the full chain rather than assembly alone.
recommendations: Support backward integration into ingot, wafer, and cell manufacturing (not just module assembly) through targeted incentives, given India's import dependence on upstream solar components.
conclusion: Building a competitive, full-chain domestic solar manufacturing base requires coordinated policy support across each stage of the value chain, not just the downstream module assembly step where most existing capacity sits.

title: Towards a Low-carbon Steel Sector: Overview of the Changing Market, Technology and Policy Context for Indian Steel
summary: Warns that CO2 emissions from India's steel sector could rise by up to 837 million tonnes by 2050 if demand growth continues on trend, and lays out a package of measures to keep the sector competitive while cutting its environmental footprint.
recommendations: Maximise use of domestic scrap steel; deploy energy-efficiency measures across mills; pursue economy-wide resource efficiency; establish pilot and demonstration plants for emerging low-carbon steelmaking technologies; and consider a phased-in emissions penalty for the sector from 2030 to signal the need for deeper decarbonization investment.
conclusion: Near-term, low-cost measures (scrap use, efficiency) can meaningfully slow emissions growth, but achieving deep decarbonization will require both new technology demonstration now and a credible long-term policy signal (such as a phased emissions penalty) to justify capital-intensive investment.

title: Decentralized Solar PV Near the Rural User End So As to Minimize Distribution Losses
summary: A field study across two contrasting feeder types — a rural network in Chhattisgarh (CSPDCL) and a semi-urban feeder in Delhi (BRPL) — examining the operational and loss-reduction benefits of siting decentralized solar PV close to the end user on distribution networks.
recommendations: Standardize the PV capacity permitted on a distribution transformer nationally, since current sanctioning limits vary by state despite transformers technically being able to absorb PV up to 100% of rating. Extend the transmission/distribution charge waivers currently given to large centralized solar parks to small decentralized systems as well, through liberal tariffs for distributed solar.
conclusion: Siting solar generation near rural and semi-urban load centres measurably reduces distribution losses, but realizing this benefit at scale requires removing regulatory inconsistencies — particularly around technical sanctioning limits and tariff treatment — that currently disadvantage small decentralized systems relative to large solar parks.

title: A Model-Based Assessment of Variable Renewable Grid Integration Costs in India
summary: Uses an hourly power system model that co-optimizes dispatch and investment to quantify the cost of integrating variable renewable energy (VRE) in India, across four scenario families varying demand, RE deployment, cost of capital, and storage costs. Finds the short-term optimal VRE share is substantially higher than the level deployed at the time.
recommendations: Prioritize enhancing inter-state/inter-regional grid integration and expanding pumped hydro capacity as the most cost-effective near-term levers for absorbing rising VRE shares; treat new coal capacity additions as economically unviable given projected costs, while retaining a limited role for gas and brownfield pumped hydro for seasonal balancing.
conclusion: Even in the short term, a substantially higher VRE share than the current trajectory is the lower-cost option for India, provided grid integration and seasonal-balancing infrastructure are developed in step with renewable deployment.

title: Renewable Power Pathways: Modelling the Integration of Wind and Solar in India by 2030
summary: A landmark modelling report charting a cost-effective, technically feasible pathway for India to reach VRE generation shares above 30% (45%+ including large hydro and nuclear) by 2030, provided a comprehensive flexibility portfolio is deployed. Estimates India will need roughly 120 GWh of battery storage by 2030.
recommendations: Shift policy focus from renewable capacity targets alone toward a comprehensive system-flexibility strategy — described as needing something like a 'National Power System Flexibility Mission.' In the medium term, source most flexibility from the existing coal and hydro fleet's operating range, complemented by fast-growing battery storage, since batteries and coal flexibility are complementary rather than competing options.
conclusion: India's 2030 renewable ambitions are achievable at no extra system cost, but only if flexibility — not just capacity — becomes the central planning objective; without a dedicated flexibility strategy, the renewable targets are at risk of faltering.

title: The Potential Role of Hydrogen in India – 'Harnessing the Hype'
summary: A first-of-its-kind cross-sector assessment of how hydrogen technologies could support India's transition to a zero-carbon energy system, based on extensive engagement with industry, power, and transport stakeholders. Projects hydrogen demand could grow five-fold by 2050, with green hydrogen costs falling over 50% by 2030.
recommendations: Target hydrogen deployment specifically at sectors where direct electrification is not viable — heavy-duty/long-distance transport, certain industrial processes, and long-duration seasonal storage in the power sector — rather than treating it as a universal decarbonization tool. Be proactive in building domestic electrolyser manufacturing capacity to capture the emerging market opportunity, given India's low-cost labour and large domestic market.
conclusion: Green hydrogen is a genuine but sector-specific opportunity for India, not a universal substitute for direct electrification; its value depends heavily on system context, and capturing the associated industrial opportunity requires early, deliberate manufacturing policy.

title: Mapping the Impact of Coal Mines and Their Closure: A Case of Betul
summary: A district-level case study of the Pathakhera Coalfield (Western Coalfields Ltd) in Betul, Madhya Pradesh, mapping the socio-economic dependence of the local community on coal mining and the likely impacts of eventual mine closure, based on field research and stakeholder consultation.
recommendations: Take a tailor-made, district-specific approach centred on strengthening rural incomes, agriculture, and education/skill-building rather than a generic closure template. Converge state and public-sector-undertaking efforts and pool available financial resources (District Mineral Foundation receipts, MPGATSVA, CSR, and transit fee revenues) to fund transition support for affected communities.
conclusion: Coal mine closure in Betul poses a significant but locally specific socio-economic risk that has not yet entered political or public discourse in the region; a coordinated, place-based transition plan — not just financial compensation — is needed well ahead of closure.

title: Bending the Curve: 2025 Forecasts for Electricity Demand by Sector and State in the Light of the COVID Epidemic
summary: Forecasts a persistent, COVID-19-driven downward revision to India's 2025 electricity demand trajectory. In the central scenario, electricity demand in India's 10 largest consuming states is projected to be roughly 5–15% lower by 2025 than pre-pandemic trend forecasts, given the close historical link between GDP growth and demand growth.
recommendations: Revise near-term capacity planning and investment decisions to account for a persistent (not merely transient) downward shift in demand growth across most states, rather than assuming a full rebound to the pre-COVID trend.
conclusion: The pandemic's economic shock is expected to leave a lasting mark on India's electricity demand trajectory to 2025, with implications for how aggressively capacity and grid investment should be scaled in the near term.

title: Discussion Paper on 'Roadmap to India's 2030 Decarbonization Target'
summary: Proposes feasible pathways for India to meet the decarbonization targets announced at COP26 Glasgow — 500 GW non-fossil capacity and 50% of energy from renewables by 2030 — requiring roughly 340 GW of additional non-fossil capacity this decade at an average of 40–43 GW/year.
recommendations: Move away from kilowatt-scale competitive bidding for village-level solar toward an attractive, SERC-approved feed-in tariff to unlock decentralized generation and private investment. Prioritize state-level leadership in developing pumped storage plants, scale up utility wind and solar bidding, and introduce the power-system flexibility needed to absorb the resulting renewable share. Invest in power-system studies and R&D collaboration on new storage technologies.
conclusion: India's COP26 targets are ambitious but achievable, and may even represent a lower-cost pathway to meeting growing energy demand — provided storage development (especially pumped storage) and supportive tariff design for decentralized generation are treated as first-order priorities, not afterthoughts.

title: Concentrating Solar Power Plants with Storage: Deployment Essential Now
summary: Building on TERI's 2030 Decarbonization Roadmap, this report focuses specifically on concentrating solar power (CSP) with thermal storage as a dispatchable renewable technology, and sets out the roadmap of actions needed to develop CSP capacity in India in support of the 500 GW non-fossil target.
recommendations: Begin CSP deployment now rather than deferring it, given the long development lead times for large storage-backed solar projects and the urgency of the 2030 non-fossil capacity target; treat CSP as a distinct storage-and-dispatchability asset class alongside batteries and pumped storage.
conclusion: CSP with thermal storage can deliver power on demand and is an attractive but currently under-deployed storage technology for India; realizing its potential requires immediate policy and project action rather than waiting for later in the decade.

title: Pumped Storage Plants – Essential for India's Energy Transition
summary: Makes the case for large-scale pumped storage plant (PSP) development as the first priority among energy storage options for India, following the Ministry of Power's April 2023 guidelines to promote PSPs. Notes India's estimated on-river PSP potential of ~103 GW, against only 4.75 GW installed at the time (3.3 GW operational in pumping mode).
recommendations: Accelerate development of both on-river and off-river pumped storage projects to keep pace with rapidly growing solar capacity, leveraging PSPs' 40+ year lifetime and 70–80% round-trip efficiency as a mature, cost-effective grid-storage option compared to emerging battery technologies.
conclusion: Large-scale pumped storage development is essential — not optional — for reliably integrating India's rapidly growing solar capacity and maintaining grid stability as VRE share rises; the technology is mature and the resource base is large, but development has lagged far behind need.

title: India's Electricity Transition Pathways to 2050: Scenarios and Insights
summary: Examines mid-century electricity transition pathways for India using two demand scenarios (Baseline and Low Carbon) and three supply scenarios (Constrained RE, Unconstrained RE, and No Fossil-fuel Scenario) out to 2050. Projects roughly fourfold growth in electricity demand and USD 1.2–1.6 trillion in new investment by mid-century, with renewables and batteries becoming cheaper than fossil generation system-wide well before 2050.
recommendations: Treat renewable-resource land availability, storage duration (daily and seasonal), and transmission scale-up as the binding constraints for deep decarbonization planning, not generation cost. In the No Fossil-fuel Scenario, prioritize longer-duration battery storage supported by pumped hydro to manage both daily and seasonal intermittency as coal phases down after 2030. Coordinate power-sector planning across centre and state given the increasing complexity from renewables, batteries, and EV load growth.
conclusion: India's power sector faces a fourfold demand increase and a multi-trillion-dollar investment requirement by 2050; while renewables are set to be the cheapest option well before then, realizing a fully decarbonized system depends on solving land, storage-duration, and transmission constraints — which now require a longer planning horizon and closer centre–state coordination than current practice.

title: Just Transition Framework for a Sustainable Future in India's Coal Mining Regions
summary: Develops a national Just Transition Framework — grounded in procedural, distributive, and restorative justice — for India's coal mining regions, informed by research in the eastern coal belt and stakeholder engagement. Proposes a two-pronged approach of institutional/governance reform plus targeted interventions on consensus-building, socio-economic transformation, and environmentally sound development, phased toward India's 2070 net-zero target.
recommendations: Establish just-transition task forces at three governance levels: national (financing and policy coordination), state (regional development planning covering mine closures, revenue loss, and skilling — a state subject), and local/district (accountability bodies including PRI/municipality representatives, civil society, unions, and coal company officials) to ensure participatory, locally grounded implementation.
conclusion: A durable just transition in India's coal regions requires coordinated action across national, state, and local governance levels simultaneously, with a comprehensive stakeholder map, phased milestones to 2070, and a monitoring mechanism — not a one-off compensation package.

title: India's Journey to Net Zero: A Conceptual Framework for Analysis
summary: A preliminary conceptual framework analyzing how India's major GHG-emitting sectors — electricity, transport, industry, agriculture, and residential cooking — could decouple growth from carbon emissions en route to net zero by 2070, assuming India's per-capita income and consumption converge toward developed-economy levels.
recommendations: Develop a distinct decoupling strategy for each major emitting sector rather than a single economy-wide lever, since the 'inflection points' where growth and emissions decouple differ by sector. Engage non-state actors, including industry coalitions such as TERI's own Industry Charter for Near-Zero Emissions, as central partners in sectoral planning and resource allocation.
conclusion: India faces the joint challenge of continued economic development and a 2070 net-zero commitment; achieving both requires sector-specific decoupling strategies developed now, since earlier decoupling of growth from emissions lowers the eventual cost of reaching net zero.

title: Solar Plus Storage: Cost Analysis of Round-the-Clock Supply for a Typical Day
summary: A techno-economic cost analysis of combining solar PV with battery energy storage systems (BESS) and pumped storage plants (PSP) to deliver round-the-clock power supply for a typical day, including a case study cost breakdown for a Delhi distribution utility (BRPL).
recommendations: Use co-located solar-plus-storage configurations sized to the specific duration of supply needed (peaking vs. full round-the-clock), since cost rises sharply with storage duration; benchmark BESS and PSP costs jointly when planning round-the-clock renewable supply for distribution utilities.
conclusion: Round-the-clock solar-plus-storage supply is becoming cost-competitive for Indian distribution utilities, but the economics are highly sensitive to the storage duration required, making duration-matched system design essential.

title: Knowledge Paper on 'Powering Progress: Unlocking the Energy Potential of Eastern and North-Eastern India'
org: TERI (commissioned by Indian Chamber of Commerce)
summary: The first integrated clean-energy roadmap for Eastern and North-Eastern India (Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Sikkim, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura), built around policy levers including RDSS, the Green Hydrogen Mission, and the BESS Viability-Gap Fund, with a phased action plan spanning 2025–47.
recommendations: Fast-track pumped storage plant development in the region — including converting mine-void/abandoned mine sites into closed-loop PSPs and building small hydro-linked pumped storage downstream of existing hydropower — targeting a quarter of India's national PSP need by 2032, while running early BESS pilots to pave the way for grid-scale batteries.
conclusion: Eastern and North-Eastern India hold outsized, currently underused potential to drive India's clean-energy transition — particularly through storage — but capturing it requires a phased 2025–2047 roadmap (Foundation, Scale & Innovate, Consolidate) rather than a single national policy applied uniformly.

title: Reassessment of Solar Potential in India: A Macro-level Study
summary: Revisits India's national solar potential and estimates it at 10,830 GW — far above MNRE's 2014 estimate of 748 GW — by broadening the assessment beyond barren/unculturable land (4,909 GW) to include floating solar (100 GW), rooftop solar, Agri-PV, and other urban-integrated and innovative applications.
recommendations: Use this substantially larger resource base to inform long-term (2050–2070) capacity planning, and prioritize innovative, non-traditional application categories — floating solar, Agri-PV, and urban-integrated solar — that were excluded from earlier, narrower potential estimates but face fewer land-use conflicts.
conclusion: India's usable solar resource base is far larger than previously assumed once innovative deployment categories are counted, removing land availability as the binding constraint on long-term solar expansion and shifting the challenge toward deployment financing and grid integration.

title: India's Nuclear Energy Vision: Strategic Pathways for SMR Deployment
summary: Examines the regulatory, institutional, and market pathways needed to support India's ambition of 100 GW nuclear capacity by 2047 (Viksit Bharat), with a particular focus on enabling deployment of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) alongside large conventional reactors, following the 2025 SHANTI Act opening the sector to private participation.
recommendations: Evolve nuclear regulation — currently designed around large reactors — to accommodate SMRs and private-sector participation; build a skilled nuclear workforce and public awareness/confidence programs; mobilize the estimated ₹23–25 lakh crore investment needed (~₹1.0–1.2 lakh crore/year) through phased combination of large reactors and SMRs to deliver firm, round-the-clock low-carbon power that complements variable renewables.
conclusion: Reaching India's 100 GW nuclear target by 2047 is achievable but requires urgent, parallel action on regulation, financing, workforce, and public acceptance — with SMRs positioned as a necessary complement to large reactors, not a replacement, particularly to provide firm baseload during non-solar hours as renewable penetration rises.
